svg.aria-label: Diagram: why internal versus external and static versus ephemeral are two independent axes, what each VM lifecycle event does to each address type including the release of ephemeral addresses on stop and the survival of static ones, how billing follows the binding rather than the usage so that an unused reserved address costs twice the in-use rate, and why a VM never sees its own external address because it is a one-to-one NAT configuration
svg.title: IP addresses: two axes, two bindings, and a bill that is highest when nothing is running
svg.text: Static and ephemeral are not two grades of permanence. They bind to different events.
Ephemeral binds to the VM running. Static binds to the VM existing. Billing follows the binding.
Two independent axes, routinely conflated
INTERNAL vs EXTERNAL is about reachability: internal cannot be reached from the internet and
is not publicly routable; external is publicly advertised and reachable by any host.
STATIC vs EPHEMERAL is about lifecycle, and is orthogonal. Internal can be either too.
Both appear and behave the same in most contexts — which is why the difference surprises.
What each lifecycle event actually does
VM RUNNING — both in use. No difference at all.
VM STOPPED — ephemeral is RELEASED and lost; static stays, and still counts as in use.
VM DELETED — ephemeral released; static survives as RESERVED but NOT in use.
Static is in use if associated with a VM whether the instance is running or stopped.
Ephemeral is in use only when the associated VM instance is running.
The billing follows the binding, not the usage
In use on a standard VM: $0.005 per hour. In use on preemptible or Spot: $0.0025.
Assigned but UNUSED: $0.01 per hour — twice the in-use rate, for an address doing nothing.
So deleting the VM and keeping the reservation DOUBLES what that address costs.
Free: all internal addresses, static or ephemeral. Static external on a forwarding rule.
Free: external IPv6 ranges on subnets, and external IPv6 on VM instances.
And the VM never sees its own external address
A VM external IPv4 is a ONE-TO-ONE NAT configuration — ONE_TO_ONE_NAT in the API.
The guest OS sees only the internal address. Nothing on the instance reports the public one.
Internal DNS resolves the instance FQDN to its INTERNAL addresses, and only inside the VPC.
So the external address is a property of the network, not of the machine.
gcloud compute addresses list shows STATUS as IN_USE or RESERVED. RESERVED is the one to
audit: it is billed, it is attached to nothing, and no VM inventory will ever show it.
The cheapest-looking state — nothing running — is the dearest. Reserve an address because
you need THAT address, never as a precaution, and release it when the resource is gone.
